Extraction: An adaptive agentic AI framework for counterfactual validation and adversarial lookahead in automated incident response (title page, p. 1). The proposed framework is named CIPHER-A — Counterfactual Incident Response Planning with Hallucination-Aware Evaluation and Reasoning — Adaptive (Abstract, p. 1).

Sheetal Prasad Kizhakel (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore, Tamil Nadu, India) and Sagar Dhanraj Pande (Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, Symbiosis Institute of Technology, Pune Campus, Symbiosis International (Deemed University), Pune, India; corresponding author) (p. 1).

Industrial SOAR platforms (Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR, Splunk SOAR, IBM QRadar) respond via pre-coded playbooks and cannot generalize to dynamic multi-stage APT attacks (§1, p. 2), while current LLM-integrated tools (Microsoft Security Copilot, Google Chronicle AI) generate a response plan once at alert ingestion and execute it sequentially, applying LLM solutions without considering the danger those actions pose to live systems and treating threats as static attacks rather than dynamic adversarial processes — 'blind execution' (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). A systematic comparison of 25 works from 2022-2026 (Table 1, pp. 4-5) identifies three unaddressed gaps: (i) no pre-execution counterfactual validation of response actions, (ii) no post-execution adversarial state update closing the loop on the remaining plan, and (iii) no dynamic attacker model of adaptation between response steps (§2.2, pp. 7-8).

CIPHER-A, an agentic AI closed-loop pipeline of five components (Table 3, p. 15) orchestrated as a LangGraph v0.2 typed state graph with conditional routing (§4.5, p. 13): AISNA normalizes Wazuh 4.7 SIEM alerts into the incident state tuple s=(A,N,U,T,Psi) (§4.5, pp. 12-13); the Counterfactual Validation Engine (CVE, Claude 3 Sonnet API) generates K=3 LLM outcome scenarios per proposed action and computes a Risk Score and a Composite Validation Score CVS = alpha*RS + beta*C (asset criticality) + gamma*U (urgency) (Eqs. 1-3, p. 10), routing each action to EXECUTE / MODIFY / ESCALATE against calibrated thresholds tau_low=0.35 and tau_high=0.65 before any live system change (Eq. 4, §4.2, p. 11); the Attacker Simulation Agent (ASA, Mistral-7B-Instruct deployed locally) predicts the adversary state transition after each executed action, grounded in MITRE ATT&CK v14.1 (14 tactics, 190+ techniques), and feeds the updated threat state into the next validation cycle (§4.3, p. 11); the Execution Dispatcher executes validated actions via live CrowdStrike Falcon API v2.0, AWS IAM/EC2 and Microsoft Active Directory LDAP APIs; and the Audit & Re-validation Controller persists every step to PostgreSQL 16 and triggers replanning when the running RPDR exceeds 0.30 (§4.5, p. 13; Table 3, p. 15). The agentic role is autonomous validated execution with calibrated human-in-the-loop escalation (ESCALATE suspends the graph and notifies an analyst, §4.5, p. 13), i.e., a safety-gated autonomous responder rather than a purely advisory copilot.

Framework construction plus controlled quantitative evaluation of a Python 3.11 prototype on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB host (§4.6, p. 15). Three public datasets (Table 2, p. 9): DARPA OPTC as primary (143 incident traces, 3 APT scenarios — lateral movement, privilege escalation + exfiltration, C2 + ransomware — across 500+ enterprise hosts; §5, p. 16), MITRE ATT&CK v14.1 as adversarial knowledge base, and CTU-13 for collateral-damage validation (847 blocking tests, §5.3, p. 20). Six system configurations analyze the identical 143 alerts through the identical Wazuh 4.7 ingestion pipeline, 'creating a controlled environment for the experiment' (§5, p. 16): three internal baselines executed by the authors in one unified environment — Baseline SOAR (rule-based, no LLM), LLM-SOAR (no pre-execution validation) and CIPHER-static (CVE-only ablation) (§5.4, p. 22) — plus two external adaptive baselines, Liu [10] (MA-LLM-IR) and Babar et al. [23] (HRL-CIDR), whose RPDR/FSR/EA/MTTC values were NOT originally reported by those authors but were derived by the present authors applying CIPHER-A's scoring framework to each paper's published performance indicators, explicitly flagged as 'indicative rather than directly comparable' and 'not independently replicable' (§5.1, p. 17; §5.4, pp. 21-23). Metrics: the new RPDR (Eq. 6, p. 12), cross-validated at 97.2% agreement against DARPA OPTC red-team ground-truth pivot logs (§4.4, p. 12), False Safety Rate (FSR), Escalation Accuracy (EA) and MTTC; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on n=143 incidents (Table 8, p. 20); weights/thresholds calibrated by grid search on an OPTC validation split of n=92 (§4.1, p. 10; §4.2, p. 11) with one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis (§5.5, pp. 23-24).

The paper reports neither MTTD nor MTTR by name: detection is delegated to the Wazuh SIEM (MTTD out of scope), and the time metric is MTTC — mean time to contain, from alert ingestion to full containment, in minutes (Table 7 note, §5.2, p. 18) — a containment-side proxy for MTTR. CIPHER-A reduces MTTC from 14.3 ± 2.1 min (Baseline SOAR) to 8.9 ± 1.4 min, a 37.8% reduction (Table 5, p. 16; Table 7, p. 19; Fig. 6, p. 20; Abstract, p. 1); this baseline is an author-implemented rule-based playbook system executed on the same 143 OPTC alerts in the same environment, i.e., an executed internal comparison (§5, p. 16; §5.4, p. 22). Decomposition: 2.1 min automated pipeline (7.2 actions x 2.45 s) plus 6.8 min analyst review on the 8.3% escalated actions, versus 14.3 min with 100% manual review in Baseline SOAR (Table 5, p. 16). Ablation: adding the CVE alone cuts MTTC from 11.8 (LLM-SOAR) to 10.2 min (-13.6% relative); adding the ASA cuts it further to 8.9 min (-12.7% relative) (§5.2, p. 19). Against the external indicative baselines, CIPHER-A's 8.9 min compares with 12.6 ± 1.8 min derived for Liu [10] and 11.1 ± 1.7 min derived for Babar et al. [23] (a 19.8% MTTC improvement) — figures computed by the present authors from those papers' published indicators, not reported by the original works (§5.4, p. 22; Table 7, p. 19). Wilcoxon MTTC tests versus the three internal baselines are all significant at p < 0.001 (Table 8, p. 20). Supporting safety/quality results: mean RPDR 15.6% vs 64.4% (Baseline SOAR) and 38.2% (CIPHER-static; 59.2% relative reduction), FSR 3.2% vs 22.7% baseline (a sevenfold reduction, §6, p. 25), EA 91.7% (Tables 6-7, pp. 17 and 19).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Claims three firsts for agentic security automation: the first pre-execution consequence-prediction mechanism for individual IR actions (CVE), the first use of MITRE ATT&CK as a grounding constraint for real-time adversarial state prediction inside an active IR pipeline (ASA), and RPDR as the first quantitative metric operationalizing the necessity of adaptive sequential re-validation (§1.1, pp. 3-6). Demonstrates a heterogeneous two-LLM agent design — cloud Claude 3 Sonnet for validation reasoning plus local Mistral-7B for low-latency adversary simulation — wired as LangGraph conditional nodes, with quantified operating cost (~700 tokens and 2.45 s per action; mean 8,330 tokens per incident; Tables 4-5, pp. 15-16). The ablation shows complementary agent roles: the CVE contributes the larger share of the FSR reduction (61.2%) while the ASA feedback loop contributes the larger share of the RPDR reduction (56.4%) (§5.2, pp. 19-20). ASA attacker-adaptation prediction reaches 78.6-84.1% accuracy per scenario and the CVE attains 94.3% collateral-damage prediction accuracy on 847 CTU-13 blocking tests (95% CI [92.5, 95.6]) (§5.3, pp. 20-21; Fig. 7, p. 21). The paper also delineates itself from the concurrent AgentSOC [24]: defender-action counterfactuals with live execution APIs versus attacker-path counterfactuals in dry-run mode (§2.1, p. 7).

The external baseline comparisons (Liu [10], Babar et al. [23]) are indicative cross-framework estimates computed by the present authors and 'cannot serve as independently replicable evaluations' (§5.4, pp. 22-23); the CVE/ASA ablation attribution is incremental within a fixed sequence, not an interaction-free causal estimate (§5.2, pp. 19-20). A residual 15.6% RPDR persists where ASA prediction confidence fell below the 0.7 update threshold (§5.1, p. 18). The prototype ran on a single A100 host without concurrent-incident stress testing; Claude API rate limits, single-GPU Mistral-7B capacity, execution-API quotas, PostgreSQL contention and analyst availability are expected bottlenecks, and the authors warn the 8.9-minute MTTC 'should not be extrapolated' to larger or highly concurrent environments until load tests are performed (§5.6, pp. 24-25). The first-hop-only subgraph fallback for highly connected hosts may omit second-hop dependencies and reduce collateral-damage accuracy (§4.2, p. 11; §5.6, p. 24), and DARPA OPTC is a controlled APT simulation with weights calibrated on a single n=92 split (§4.1, p. 10). Future work: knowledge-graph encodings of topology for blast-radius analysis, federated CIPHER-A sharing ASA forecasts across organizations, and formal causal models replacing probabilistic LLM estimates (§7, p. 25). The authors used GPT-4 to improve language clarity (Declarations, p. 26).

High relevance: this is one of the four primary studies in the nominal-times cluster reporting response-time metrics against a baseline. It provides an executed, controlled empirical comparison — six configurations over the identical 143 DARPA OPTC alerts and ingestion pipeline (§5, p. 16) — in which an agentic pipeline with human-in-the-loop escalation reduces MTTC from 14.3 to 8.9 min (-37.8%, Table 5, p. 16; Table 7, p. 19) with Wilcoxon p < 0.001 (Table 8, p. 20), satisfying Art. I for the containment-time claim against the concrete internal Baseline SOAR. It directly evidences the thesis mechanism: safety-gated agentic validation plus selective escalation (8.3% of actions, 91.7% accuracy) removes the human-review bottleneck that dominates containment time, i.e., the MTTR side of the thesis; MTTD is not addressed since detection is delegated to the SIEM (§5.2, p. 18). Mandatory caveats: the venue (Discover Artificial Intelligence) is Qualis A3, below the review's A1-A2 preferred threshold, so the study enters under the stratum waiver PDR-0007; and all figures attributed to the external baselines Liu [10] and Babar et al. [23] are author-derived indicative estimates (§5.4, pp. 21-23), so only the internal comparisons (Baseline SOAR, LLM-SOAR, CIPHER-static) count as executed empirical evidence under Art. I.

High — it delivers an executed baseline comparison with nominal containment-time numbers (MTTC 14.3 -> 8.9 min, -37.8%, p < 0.001) on a public enterprise-scale APT dataset, with an agentic human-in-the-loop architecture squarely in the thesis scope. The Qualis A3 stratum (PDR-0007) and the indicative nature of the external baselines temper, but do not negate, its evidentiary weight.
